atoms.1: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is treated with a combination of antibiotics.
atoms.2: The antibiotics used for PID target likely causative organisms.
atoms.3: Likely causative organisms for PID include N. gonorrhoeae.
atoms.4: Likely causative organisms for PID include C. trachomatis.
atoms.5: Likely causative organisms for PID include gram-negative bacteria.
atoms.6: Likely causative organisms for PID include anaerobes.
atoms.7: Likely causative organisms for PID include Group B streptococcus.
atoms.8: Likely causative organisms for PID include genital mycoplasmas.
atoms.9: The treatment regimens for PID should ensure broad-spectrum coverage.
atoms.10: Ensuring broad-spectrum coverage addresses the polymicrobial nature of PID.
atoms.11: Patients with mild to moderately severe acute PID can be treated as outpatients.
atoms.12: Clinical outcomes among women treated with oral therapy for PID are similar to those treated with parenteral therapy.
atoms.13: Patients with PID who do not improve within 72 hours of starting oral therapy should be reassessed.
atoms.14: Patients with PID who do not improve within 72 hours of starting oral therapy may need intravenous therapy.
atoms.15: Intravenous therapy for PID may be administered on an outpatient or inpatient basis.
atoms.16: For patients requiring inpatient treatment for PID, the CDC recommends a combination of clindamycin and gentamicin.
atoms.17: For patients requiring inpatient treatment for PID, the CDC recommends a combination of cefoxitin and doxycycline.
atoms.18: Hospitalization for PID should be considered if the patient is severely ill.
atoms.19: Hospitalization for PID should be considered if the patient is pregnant.
atoms.20: Hospitalization for PID should be considered if the patient is unable to follow or tolerate an outpatient regimen.
atoms.21: Hospitalization for PID should be considered if the patient has failed outpatient therapy.
atoms.22: Hospitalization for PID should be considered if a surgical emergency cannot be excluded.
atoms.23: A common oral/outpatient regimen for PID includes a single intramuscular dose of cefoxitin (2 g) with oral doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 14 days).
atoms.24: The addition of metronidazole (500 mg twice daily for 14 days) to an oral/outpatient regimen can provide coverage for anaerobes.
atoms.25: The addition of metronidazole (500 mg twice daily for 14 days) to an oral/outpatient regimen can treat bacterial vaginosis associated with PID.
atoms.26: An effective inpatient regimen for PID includes intravenous cefoxitin (2 g every 6 hours) combined with doxycycline (100 mg orally or intravenously every 12 hours) until 24 hours after clinical improvement.
atoms.27: After clinical improvement, the inpatient regimen for PID is followed by oral doxycycline to complete a 14-day course.
atoms.28: Another effective inpatient regimen for PID includes intravenous clindamycin (900 mg every 8 hours) with gentamicin (loading dose of 2 mg/kg body weight followed by 1.5 mg/kg every 8 hours).
atoms.29: Close follow-up for PID is crucial to ensure resolution of symptoms.
atoms.30: Close follow-up for PID is crucial to prevent long-term complications.
atoms.31: Patients with PID should be reevaluated within 72 hours of starting treatment to confirm clinical improvement.
atoms.32: Evaluation and treatment of male sexual partners are imperative to prevent reinfection of PID.
atoms.33: Early diagnosis and treatment of acute PID are essential to minimize long-term sequelae.
atoms.34: Long-term sequelae of PID include chronic pelvic pain.
atoms.35: Long-term sequelae of PID include tubal infertility.
atoms.36: Long-term sequelae of PID include ectopic pregnancy.
atoms.37: Improved diagnostic techniques are needed to further reduce complications of PID.
atoms.38: Improved treatment modalities are needed to further reduce complications of PID.
